To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we observed a positive association between age when adult height is attained and glioma risk.
older age at the completion adult height is associated with an overall increased risk of gliomas and with a greater risk of lower grade non-gioblastomas.
older age at attainment of height was associated with a significantly increased risk of adult-onset glioma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the growth phase and the occurrence of glioma.
the association of age at attainment of height and glioma.
the relationship between growth and development during adolescence and the development of glioma in adulthood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
older age at attainment of height completion is associated with increased risk of adult-onset glioma.
the association between age at height completion and glioma risk is not well established.
the association between age at attainment adult height and gliomas is positive and statistically significant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the adolescent growth phase is an important window in the development of adult glioma.
a prolonged adolescent growth spurt is associated with an increase in glioma risk.
older age at the completion (i.e., cessation) of linear growth is an independent risk factor for the development of glioma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a longer period of growth in adolescence, and the associated higher levels of circulating growth factors, may be associated with a greater risk of adult gliomas.
the adolescent growth phase is a critical period of development for brain growth, and that a prolonged growth phase may be a risk factor for glioma in adults.
there is a strong association between the timing of growth and glioma risk and the association appears to be consistent for men and women and for all categories of adult height.
